A C^1 support change shifts both endpoints of every exposed face by the same bounded small vector; unchanged support and derivative at component endpoints make the old and new arcs share endpoints. Their difference is a closed path confined to that strict halfplane, so it contributes zero winding on the opposite side. If the interval union is the entire circle, connectedness gives the one sign on the whole old and new boundaries. The first-area functional on each component is linear, so assigning its common bit yields the sum of the individual first cap responses, even for overlapping acceleration tests. The quadratic area form gives second coefficient B_j+T_j(E) in units t squared over two: G–E cross terms start at order three, and disjoint generator supports remove cross terms within G. Finite domination constants and positive inactive-row margins suffice for feasibility of the combined path; each active row is identically annihilated by its own potential.

The finite fixed halfspace traces cover every sampled plane after the perturbation, so a simultaneous strict cap-fraction drop lowers the actual maximal normalized depth. Homogeneity gives a nonzero nonnegative separator; its value on the acceleration subspace is zero because both signs occur. Normalizing its sum to one gives weights lambda=pi/beta and the quadratic value beta times the asserted restricted form.

On a guard, for fixed kernel v the signed measure uses only affected coordinates with constant W. Enlarge the potential interval inside the guard so the compact source support avoids its endpoints. The diffuse locality result annihilates the atomless part on the source support, and each source is a positive multiple of a restriction of R. Taking a finite basis for each kernel and then the countable exhaustion preserves one common weight vector.

For continuous positive radii, r=rho/sum rho lies in the kernel, so testing the annihilation with r gives the squared-radius identity. The support-point map has derivative rho times the unit tangent. Each fixed line has at most two contacts with a strictly convex fiber; tangencies have no bit jump. The continuous densities allow both one-sided limits, whose difference is the stated weighted jump. Every transverse contribution of one cap at one angle has the same sign across all fibers, so an opposite nonzero contribution requires a different positive-weight cap.
